A fix that was tested is missing from the commit. Root cause: the file was edited after the last git add, and the commit is written from the index.
Believing an empty "Changes to be committed" means an empty index. Root cause: with nothing staged, the index describes the same tree as HEAD.
Assuming an unstaged secret left no trace. Root cause: unstaging removes the entry, not the object; the blob remains until garbage collection.
Panicking that the unstaged secret was pushed. Root cause: forgetting what a push sends: the objects that the pushed commits need, and no commit refers to that blob.

beats.text: Neither. They tested different things. The commit contained what was in the index, and CI, the server that tests every commit, ran that. Your own tests ran against something else: the files on disk.
beats.tele: Neither. They tested different things. The commit contained what was in the index, and CI, the server that tests every commit, ran that. Your own tests ran against something else: the files on disk.

beats.text: Git doesn't build a commit from your files. It builds it from the index, a second complete record of the project that sits between the working tree and HEAD. The working tree is the files on your disk, and HEAD is your last commit, the last saved snapshot. Understanding usually stops at this layer.

beats.text: In one sentence. The index is a single file, .git/index, that lists every tracked path together with the ID of a blob, and git commit turns exactly that list into the tree of the new commit. A blob is the object that holds one file's content. A tree is the object that records one directory.
beats.tele: In one sentence. The index is a single file, `.git/index`, that lists every tracked path together with the ID of a blob, and `git commit` turns exactly that list into the tree of the new commit. A blob is the object that holds one file's content. A tree is the object that records one directory.

beats.text: Precisely. Git's data-model document says: "The index, also known as the 'staging area', is a list of files and the contents of each file, stored as a blob". And: "Unlike a tree, the index is a flat list of files. When you commit, Git converts the list of files in the index to a directory tree and uses that tree in the new commit".
beats.tele: Precisely. Git's data-model document says: "The index, also known as the 'staging area', is a list of files and the contents of each file, stored as a blob". And: "Unlike a tree, the index is a flat list of files. When you commit, Git converts the list of files in the index to a directory tree and uses that tree in the new commit".

beats.text: Each entry has four fields. The file type and mode. The blob ID. A stage number, which is 0 except during a conflict. And the full path. Mode, blob ID and path are what the commit's tree receives. Each entry also carries bookkeeping that never leaves your machine: cached filesystem data, and flag bits. Video 18 opens both. The old name "cache" survives in options such as --cached.
beats.tele: Each entry has four fields. The file type and mode. The blob ID. A stage number, which is 0 except during a conflict. And the full path. Mode, blob ID and path are what the commit's tree receives. Each entry also carries bookkeeping that never leaves your machine: cached filesystem data, and flag bits. Video 18 opens both. The old name "cache" survives in options such as `--cached`.

beats.text: The correction. The definition corrects the most common wrong model. Nothing in the index is a "change". "Staged changes" are the result of comparing the index with HEAD. And an index with nothing staged is not empty: it describes the same tree as HEAD.
beats.tele: The correction. The definition corrects the most common wrong model. Nothing in the index is a "change". "Staged changes" are the result of comparing the index with HEAD. And an index with nothing staged is not empty: it describes the same tree as HEAD.

beats.text: Inside .git. One binary file, created by the first git add: a 12-byte header, the entries sorted by path, optional extensions, and a checksum.
beats.tele: Inside `.git`. One binary file, created by the first `git add`: a 12-byte header, the entries sorted by path, optional extensions, and a checksum.

beats.text: What git add writes. In one sentence: git add <path> stores the current content of the file as a blob in the object database, Git's store inside the dot git folder, and writes that blob's ID into the path's index entry. It's a copy taken at that moment, not a subscription to the file.
beats.tele: What `git add` writes. In one sentence: `git add <path>` stores the current content of the file as a blob in the object database, Git's store inside the dot git folder, and writes that blob's ID into the path's index entry. It's a copy taken at that moment, not a subscription to the file.

beats.text: The manual: "It only adds the content of the specified file(s) at the time the add command is run; if you want subsequent changes included in the next commit, then you must run git add again".
beats.tele: The manual: "It only adds the content of the specified file(s) at the time the add command is run; if you want subsequent changes included in the next commit, then you must run `git add` again".

beats.text: Two things are written: one object, unless an identical blob already exists, and one index entry. No ref moves, meaning no branch name, so no reflog, Git's journal of such moves, records an add. git add is 🟢 SAFE: it writes a blob and an index entry.

beats.text: The root cause from the hook. A fix that was tested but is missing from the commit was edited after the last git add. The commit is written from the index, which still held the earlier version. Status showed MM. Add the file again and commit, and read git diff --cached before every commit.

beats.text: What an add leaves behind. Unstaging removes the entry, not the object. The blob that git add wrote stays in the object database as a dangling blob, an object that nothing refers to. A push, which sends commits to another repository, doesn't send it: a push sends what the pushed commits need, and no commit refers to this object.

beats.text: Garbage collection, Git's clean-up of unused objects, removes the stray object once it's older than gc.pruneExpire, two weeks by default. Until then it's also a rescue route: content that was staged once and then lost can be found with git fsck.

beats.text: Where this matters and where it does not. This isn't something to "use" or "not use". It's how every commit is made. The practical rule is about trust: "What exactly will be in this commit?" has one authoritative answer, the index. Reviewers, CI and every clone receive the tree that was written from it, never your working tree.

beats.text: A picture helps. The textbook's analogy: the packing list for the next shipment. It names every item that will be in the box, not the items that differ from the last box, and the warehouse ships what the list says even if the shelf has changed since.

beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Thinking the index is a list of changes. Root cause: "staged changes" is the result of comparing the index with HEAD; the index itself is a complete list of every tracked path.
beats.tele: Thinking the index is a list of changes. Root cause: "staged changes" is the result of comparing the index with HEAD; the index itself is a complete list of every tracked path.

beats.text: A fix that was tested is missing from the commit. Root cause: the file was edited after the last git add, and the commit is written from the index.
beats.tele: A fix that was tested is missing from the commit. Root cause: the file was edited after the last `git add`, and the commit is written from the index.

beats.text: Believing an empty "Changes to be committed" means an empty index. Root cause: with nothing staged, the index describes the same tree as HEAD.
beats.tele: Believing an empty "Changes to be committed" means an empty index. Root cause: with nothing staged, the index describes the same tree as HEAD.

beats.text: Assuming an unstaged secret left no trace. Root cause: unstaging removes the entry, not the object; the blob remains until garbage collection.
beats.tele: Assuming an unstaged secret left no trace. Root cause: unstaging removes the entry, not the object; the blob remains until garbage collection.

beats.text: Panicking that the unstaged secret was pushed. Root cause: forgetting what a push sends: the objects that the pushed commits need, and no commit refers to that blob.
beats.tele: Panicking that the unstaged secret was pushed. Root cause: forgetting what a push sends: the objects that the pushed commits need, and no commit refers to that blob.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. An engineer on an LLM application team runs git add . and notices in the status output that a 2 gigabyte checkpoint and an .env file were picked up. They unstage both immediately. Two questions follow, and the model answers both. Is there history to rewrite? No: a secret or a checkpoint that was added and then unstaged is in no commit and hasn't travelled.
beats.tele: Now, out of the lab. An engineer on an LLM application team runs `git add .` and notices in the status output that a 2 gigabyte checkpoint and an `.env` file were picked up. They unstage both immediately. Two questions follow, and the model answers both. Is there history to rewrite? No: a secret or a checkpoint that was added and then unstaged is in no commit and hasn't travelled.

beats.text: Is it still on the laptop? Yes, as a stray object, until garbage collection removes it once it's older than gc.pruneExpire, two weeks by default. The same fact works in your favour on a bad day: content that was staged once and then lost can be found with git fsck.
beats.tele: Is it still on the laptop? Yes, as a stray object, until garbage collection removes it once it's older than `gc.pruneExpire`, two weeks by default. The same fact works in your favour on a bad day: content that was staged once and then lost can be found with `git fsck`.

beats.text: Q27: "What exactly does git add write, and what remains of it after git restore --staged? Does a push send it?"
beats.tele: Q27: "What exactly does `git add` write, and what remains of it after `git restore --staged`? Does a push send it?"

beats.text: Answer out loud. A strong answer counts the writes and names where each lands, says which of them git restore --staged reverses and which it doesn't, and reasons about the push from the rule for what a push transfers. Say how long the leftover stays, and what removes it.
beats.tele: Answer out loud. A strong answer counts the writes and names where each lands, says which of them `git restore --staged` reverses and which it doesn't, and reasons about the push from the rule for what a push transfers. Say how long the leftover stays, and what removes it.

beats.text: Let's land this. You should now be able to say, in your own words: the index is one file that lists every tracked path with a mode and a blob ID, flat and sorted. It's a full snapshot, not a list of changes.
beats.tele: Let's land this. You should now be able to say, in your own words: the index is one file that lists every tracked path with a mode and a blob ID, flat and sorted. It's a full snapshot, not a list of changes.

beats.text: With nothing staged it describes the same tree as HEAD, and I can prove that with git write-tree. git add writes a blob and an index entry, as a copy at that moment, and later edits are not in it. git commit records the index and doesn't read the working tree.
beats.tele: With nothing staged it describes the same tree as HEAD, and I can prove that with `git write-tree`. `git add` writes a blob and an index entry, as a copy at that moment, and later edits are not in it. `git commit` records the index and doesn't read the working tree.

beats.text: Unstaging removes the entry and leaves the blob, which no push sends and which garbage collection removes later.
beats.tele: Unstaging removes the entry and leaves the blob, which no push sends and which garbage collection removes later.
